summary: PCOS (now also called PMOS by Mayo Clinic and NHS) is managed with lifestyle change (about 5% weight loss can improve symptoms; aerobic plus strength exercise for insulin resistance) and clinician-prescribed treatments: combined pill or cyclic progestin for cycles and endometrial protection, metformin, spironolactone or eflornithine for hair/acne, and letrozole or clomifene for fertility. Inositol has low-certainty evidence: an umbrella review of meta-analyses found improved androgens, SHBG and insulin resistance vs placebo and no clear difference vs metformin, while Cochrane found no clear fertility benefit (very low certainty). Spearmint tea has one small 30-day RCT showing lower testosterone but no change in objective hirsutism score. Ongoing monitoring of blood pressure, glucose, lipids, mood and sleep apnea is advised.

effective_types.type: lifestyle / weight-management program (diet + aerobic and strength exercise)
combined oral contraceptive or cyclic progestin (prescription)
letrozole or clomifene for ovulation induction (prescription)
telehealth clinician care (OB-GYN/endocrinology) that prescribes the above

caution: Spironolactone can cause birth defects; needs effective contraception and is not for pregnancy or when planning pregnancy (https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/pcos/diagnosis-treatment/drc-20353443)
Cyclic progestin therapy does not prevent pregnancy (https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/pcos/diagnosis-treatment/drc-20353443)

Inositol evidence is mostly low/very-low quality; D-chiro-inositol alone warrants caution and combination products did not consistently beat myo-inositol alone (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41757236/)
Inositol harms are poorly reported in trials, so safety is unclear (https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD012378_inositol-women-polycystic-ovary-syndrome)
Spearmint tea evidence is one 30-day trial of 42 women; it lowered testosterone but did not change objective hirsutism score (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19585478)

Irregular cycles (common in PCOS) make home LH ovulation tests harder to interpret (https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/007062.htm); PCOS can cause mildly elevated LH (https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/body/22255-luteinizing-hormone)
see_a_clinician_if: You think you may have PCOS/PMOS, or symptoms affect everyday life, work or relationships (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/polycystic-ovary-syndrome-pcos/diagnosis/)

You are diagnosed: ongoing checks of blood pressure, glucose tolerance, cholesterol/triglycerides, plus screening for depression, anxiety and sleep apnea are advised (https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/pcos/diagnosis-treatment/drc-20353443)
Irregular or absent periods, since treatment protects the uterine lining and lowers endometrial cancer risk (https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/pcos/diagnosis-treatment/drc-20353443)
Trying to conceive without success (fertility medicines such as letrozole are prescription) (https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/pcos/diagnosis-treatment/drc-20353443)
catalog_gaps: structured lifestyle / weight-management or dietitian program (telehealth or app)
myo-inositol-only supplement (umbrella review favored myo-inositol alone over combos)
at-home hair removal tools/services for hirsutism
acne skin-care products (OTC) for PCOS-related acne
mental health support / talking therapy service
at-home metabolic screening tests (glucose/HbA1c, lipids) to support recommended monitoring

summary: NICE NG73 recommends a short (about 3 month) trial of paracetamol or an NSAID as first-line pain relief, and offering hormonal treatment (combined pill or a progestogen) for suspected, confirmed or recurrent endometriosis, with referral to gynaecology or a specialist centre if symptoms persist or deep disease is suspected. Mayo Clinic adds GnRH agonists/antagonists, aromatase inhibitors and conservative surgery, and lists warm baths and a heating pad, pelvic floor physical therapy and support groups as self-care. NICE says evidence does not support traditional Chinese medicine, Chinese herbal medicines or supplements.

effective_types.type: hormonal treatment: combined pill or progestogen (prescription)
specialist / multidisciplinary gynecology care (incl. telehealth entry point) with surgery referral

caution: Hormonal treatment should not be offered to women trying to conceive; it does not improve spontaneous pregnancy rates (https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng73/resources/endometriosis-diagnosis-and-management-pdf-1837632548293)
Hormone therapy is not a permanent fix; symptoms may return after stopping (https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/endometriosis/diagnosis-treatment/drc-20354661)
Supplements and herbs can interact with standard treatment; check with the care team first (https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/endometriosis/diagnosis-treatment/drc-20354661)

Evidence does not support traditional Chinese medicine, Chinese herbal medicines or supplements for endometriosis (https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng73/resources/endometriosis-diagnosis-and-management-pdf-1837632548293)
see_a_clinician_if: Chronic pelvic pain, period pain affecting daily life, deep pain during or after sex, cyclical bowel or urinary symptoms, or infertility with any of these (https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng73/resources/endometriosis-diagnosis-and-management-pdf-1837632548293)
Symptoms are severe, persistent or recurrent, or initial treatment fails or is not tolerated (https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng73/resources/endometriosis-diagnosis-and-management-pdf-1837632548293)
Suspected deep endometriosis involving bowel, bladder or ureter (specialist centre referral) (https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng73/resources/endometriosis-diagnosis-and-management-pdf-1837632548293)
Very heavy bleeding that soaks through pads/tampons quickly, or symptoms worsen despite GP treatment (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/endometriosis/)
catalog_gaps: pelvic floor physical therapy service (in-person or telehealth)
pain and symptom diary / tracker app
reusable heating pad (in addition to disposable heat wraps)

summary: Fibroids without symptoms can be watched, as they often grow slowly and shrink after menopause. Symptomatic fibroids are treated by clinicians: GnRH agonists/antagonists, progestin IUD, tranexamic acid, low-dose pills for bleeding, NSAIDs for pain (not bleeding), iron and vitamins if heavy bleeding has caused anemia, and procedures (UAE, MRI-guided focused ultrasound, radiofrequency ablation, myomectomy, endometrial ablation, hysterectomy). Mayo Clinic states there is no scientific evidence that diets, black cohosh, herbal preparations, magnet therapy or homeopathy help.

effective_types.type: clinician-prescribed medicines (GnRH agonist/antagonist, progestin IUD, tranexamic acid, low-dose pill)
procedures (UAE, focused ultrasound, RF ablation, myomectomy, hysterectomy)
telehealth specialist care that coordinates the above
iron supplement for anemia from heavy bleeding (clinician-guided)
diets, black cohosh, herbal preparations, homeopathy, magnets

caution: GnRH agonists are usually limited to about 6 months due to bone loss (https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/uterine-fibroids/diagnosis-treatment/drc-20354294)
Endometrial ablation and UAE are generally not advised for those wanting future pregnancy (https://www.nichd.nih.gov/health/topics/uterine/conditioninfo/treatments/other-treatments)
Iron should be started with a clinician after a blood count confirms anemia (https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/uterine-fibroids/diagnosis-treatment/drc-20354294)
Herbal products such as black cohosh are not shown to help fibroids (https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/uterine-fibroids/diagnosis-treatment/drc-20354294)
see_a_clinician_if: Heavy menstrual bleeding, especially with signs of anemia (https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/uterine-fibroids/diagnosis-treatment/drc-20354294)
Irregular bleeding between periods, which may need blood tests (https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/uterine-fibroids/diagnosis-treatment/drc-20354294)
Any symptoms before choosing a treatment; options should be discussed with a provider (https://www.nichd.nih.gov/health/topics/uterine/conditioninfo/treatments/other-treatments)
catalog_gaps: heavy-flow menstrual products (high-capacity pads, cups, period underwear)

summary: Adenomyosis causes painful cramps, heavy or prolonged bleeding and pelvic pain, and is diagnosed with ultrasound or MRI. Mayo Clinic recommends ibuprofen starting 1-2 days before and during the period, hormonal options (combined pill/patch/ring, progestin IUD or continuous pills), and hysterectomy for severe refractory cases; Cleveland Clinic adds tranexamic acid. For home relief Mayo Clinic lists a warm bath and a heating pad on the lower belly. No catalog products are currently matched to this need.
caution: Endometrial biopsy cannot confirm adenomyosis; imaging and clinician assessment are needed (https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/adenomyosis/diagnosis-treatment/drc-20369143)
Heavy bleeding can cause anemia (fatigue, feeling cold) (https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/14167-adenomyosis)
see_a_clinician_if: Extremely heavy periods, severely painful cramps, painful intercourse, or abdominal fullness/heaviness (https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/14167-adenomyosis)
catalog_gaps: heat therapy: existing heat wrap product (p-thermacare) is not yet matched to this need
telehealth gynecology for adenomyosis (existing telehealth products are not matched here)

summary: No credible source opened supports at-home urine hormone panels as tools to explain or manage general hormone-related symptoms. FDA and MedlinePlus describe home urine LH/E3G tests as reasonably reliable (about 9 in 10) for detecting the hormone rise before ovulation, i.e. a fertility-timing tool, with irregular cycles, the pill and HRT affecting results. Cleveland Clinic says at-home fertility tests are not a substitute for a specialist and that ovarian reserve testing is done clinically (AMH blood test plus ultrasound). Symptoms attributed to hormones should be assessed by a clinician.

effective_types.type: clinician assessment (in person or telehealth) with blood tests as indicated
home urine LH/E3G ovulation test (for ovulation timing, not symptom diagnosis)

caution: Hormonal contraceptives and HRT lower LH and clomiphene raises it, distorting home test results (https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/007062.htm)
Home ovulation tests are not reliable for preventing pregnancy (https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/home-use-tests/ovulation-urine-test)
At-home fertility tests are not a substitute for a fertility specialist (https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/articles/fertility-test)
see_a_clinician_if: No LH surge is detected, or no pregnancy after several months of use (https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/007062.htm)
Home test results suggest conceiving may be difficult (https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/articles/fertility-test)
catalog_gaps: telehealth clinician / menopause-specialist care for hormone-related symptoms (none currently matched to this need)
symptom tracking app aimed at cycle or perimenopause symptoms (to bring to a clinician)

summary: Normal cycles run 21 to 35 days; cycles outside that range or varying by more than about 9 days are irregular, with causes ranging from puberty, perimenopause, stress, weight change and contraception to PCOS, thyroid disease and primary ovarian insufficiency. The evidence-backed first step is recording period start/end dates (app or diary) and seeing a clinician for evaluation; no OTC product regulates cycles. Urine LH ovulation kits can help show whether/when ovulation occurs, but may miss the surge in irregular cycles, and temperature (BBT) methods are inaccurate with irregular cycles.

effective_types.type: clinician evaluation (history, pelvic exam, hormone/thyroid tests, ultrasound), in person or via telehealth
period tracking app or paper diary to document cycle length, flow, spotting
urine LH ovulation predictor kit (to check ovulation, especially if trying to conceive)
basal body temperature / temperature wearables for cycle prediction
at-home FSH/menopause hormone tests (cannot diagnose perimenopause)

caution: Temperature-based fertility apps are less suitable for cycles under 21 or over 35 days; do not rely on them for contraception with irregular cycles (FDA De Novo DEN170052)
Home FSH tests do not detect menopause or perimenopause and should not be used to stop contraception (FDA home menopause test page)
Irregularity can persist up to 6 months after stopping the pill (Cleveland Clinic)
see_a_clinician_if: periods are irregular, or become very irregular after previously regular cycles (NHS; Cleveland Clinic)
irregular periods with weight gain, tiredness, facial hair growth, or oily/dry skin, possible PCOS/thyroid signs (NHS)
periods last longer than 7 days, bleeding between periods, or soaking a pad/tampon every hour for 2-3 hours (NHS; Cleveland Clinic)
irregular periods and difficulty getting pregnant (NHS); no conception after 12 months if under 35 or 6 months if 35+ (Cleveland Clinic)
severe pain or possible pregnancy (Cleveland Clinic)
catalog_gaps: basic urine LH ovulation test strips (low-cost alternative to multi-hormone monitors)
in-person OB-GYN/primary care clinician directory (ultrasound and labs needed for workup)

summary: Pregnancy is the most common cause of a missed period, so a home urine hCG test is the established first step; for best reliability test 1 to 2 weeks after the missed period and treat an early negative as tentative. Missing 3 or more periods in a row (or 6 months without a period if cycles were irregular) is secondary amenorrhea and warrants clinician evaluation. Trackers only help document that a period is late; they do not evaluate the cause.

effective_types.type: clinician evaluation after 3 missed periods (in person or telehealth)
period tracking app or diary to document missed cycles

caution: About 10 to 20 in 100 pregnant women will not test positive on the first day of a missed period; retest after several days if pregnancy is still possible (FDA pregnancy test page)
Ovulation and FSH home tests are not pregnancy tests and do not explain a missed period (FDA home menopause test page; MedlinePlus ovulation test)
see_a_clinician_if: 3 or more missed periods in a row, or no period for 6+ months with previously irregular cycles (Mayo Clinic)
missed period with unusual vaginal bleeding and tummy or pelvic pain, possible ectopic pregnancy, seek urgent care (NHS)
positive pregnancy test (FDA pregnancy test page)

summary: Spotting between periods has many causes: hormonal contraception (especially irregular pill use), IUDs, polyps, fibroids, infections such as chlamydia, cervical changes, thyroid problems, pregnancy complications, and rarely cancer, so any unexplained bleeding between periods should be checked by a clinician. Products here only contain light bleeding: liners and light-absorbency period underwear are reasonable for spotting. Note period underwear can make blood loss harder to judge, and tracking how often products are soaked helps clinicians.

effective_types.type: panty liners for light spotting containment
clinician / sexual health clinic evaluation including STI testing
tracking bleeding days and number of products used

caution: Reusable products such as period underwear reduce product changes and can leak and mask heavy bleeding, so they are not adequate as sole containment for heavy menstrual bleeding (PMC13094350 randomized trial)
Avoid aspirin when bleeding abnormally, as it may prolong bleeding (MedlinePlus)
see_a_clinician_if: any unexplained bleeding between periods or after sex (NHS; MedlinePlus)
recent missed period plus unusual bleeding and pelvic or tummy pain, possible ectopic pregnancy, urgent (NHS)
bleeding while pregnant, or any bleeding after menopause (MedlinePlus)
heavy bleeding, or bleeding with pelvic pain, fatigue or dizziness (MedlinePlus)
catalog_gaps: at-home STI (chlamydia/gonorrhea) test kits, since infection is a named cause of intermenstrual bleeding
home pregnancy test matched to spotting with a late period

summary: Diagnosis rests on a symptom diary across at least 2 cycles; lifestyle measures (exercise, sleep, limiting salt, caffeine and alcohol) are first steps. For moderate to severe PMS/PMDD, SSRIs have moderate-certainty Cochrane evidence, and hormonal contraception and CBT are clinician options. Supplements: calcium (about 1,200 mg/day) has the most consistent trial support though not uniform; vitamin B6 and chasteberry (vitex) show benefit in low-quality trials; magnesium evidence is limited; evening primrose oil and dong quai lack evidence.

effective_types.type: SSRI antidepressant via clinician (first-line for severe PMS/PMDD)
symptom diary / cycle tracker for at least 2 cycles (diagnostic tool)
vitamin B6 (e.g. 80 mg/day studied; stay at or under 100 mg/day UL)
NSAID (OTC) for cramps and breast discomfort

caution: Chasteberry may be unsafe in pregnancy or breastfeeding and may not be safe with hormone-sensitive conditions such as breast, uterine or ovarian cancer (NCCIH)
Dong quai: avoid in pregnancy (miscarriage risk) and breastfeeding; may increase bleeding risk with warfarin or antiplatelet drugs; photosensitivity (MSK; LactMed)
Vitamin B6 above 100 mg/day long term risks sensory neuropathy; EFSA set a lower 12 mg/day limit (ODS)
St. John's wort, sometimes used for PMS, can reduce birth control pill effectiveness (Mayo Clinic)
Check with a GP or pharmacist before regular supplements if taking other medicines (NHS)
see_a_clinician_if: symptoms affect daily life or lifestyle changes have not helped (NHS)
severe mood symptoms suggesting PMDD (Mayo Clinic)
PMDD symptoms with suicidal thoughts: emergency care now (NHS)
catalog_gaps: standalone calcium carbonate/citrate supplement positioned for PMS (current match is a bone-health product)
standalone vitamin B6 at a dose at or below the 100 mg UL
CBT / mental health telehealth for PMDD
period/symptom tracker apps should be matched to PMS as the diagnostic symptom diary (catalog has them, rows do not)

summary: For cyclical breast pain, NHS and Mayo recommend a well-fitting supportive bra (soft bra at night) and paracetamol/ibuprofen or a topical NSAID gel. Supplements (evening primrose oil, vitamin E, B6) show limited or mixed results, and NCCIH says evening primrose oil is probably no better than placebo. Chasteberry has some trial evidence for premenstrual breast pain but needs higher-quality studies; prescription options (danazol, tamoxifen) are for severe cases and carry significant side effects.
caution: Try one supplement at a time and stop if no improvement after a few months (Mayo Clinic)
Long-term acetaminophen/NSAID use carries liver and other side-effect risks (Mayo Clinic)
Chasteberry: avoid in pregnancy/breastfeeding and hormone-sensitive cancers (NCCIH; LactMed)
see_a_clinician_if: a hard lump that does not move, nipple discharge (possibly bloody), breast shape change, dimpled orange-peel skin, rash on the nipple or inverted nipple, urgent (NHS)
breast red, hot or swollen, or pain with high temperature or shivering, urgent (NHS)
pain not improving or painkillers not helping; family history of breast cancer; possible pregnancy (NHS)

summary: The ESNM/UEG bloating consensus gives no specific treatment for premenstrual or menstrual bloating; it only advises considering sex-hormone fluctuations as a contributor (very low evidence). Chasteberry has low-to-moderate quality evidence mainly for PMS breast tenderness, not bloating, and vitamin B6 'shows promise' for overall PMS symptoms in small, methodologically weak trials. No supplement is established specifically for cycle-related bloating.

effective_types.type: vitamin B6 (PMS symptoms overall, up to 100 mg/day UL)
general functional-bloating measures (diet review, selected probiotics)

caution: Chasteberry may be unsafe in pregnancy or breastfeeding and for women with hormone-sensitive conditions such as breast, uterine or ovarian cancer (NCCIH, https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/chasteberry)
Vitamin B6 adult UL is 100 mg/day; chronic high doses cause sensory neuropathy, and EFSA set a 12 mg/day limit (ODS, https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/VitaminB6-HealthProfessional)
see_a_clinician_if: Bloating with unexplained weight loss, severe or worsening symptoms, or other alarm signs needs evaluation to exclude organic disease such as celiac disease, pancreatic insufficiency, Crohn's, hypothyroidism, diabetes, or GI/gynecologic malignancy (ESNM/UEG consensus, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12606050/)

Gas or bloating that suddenly changes, or comes with abdominal pain, constipation, diarrhea or weight loss (NIDDK, https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/gas-digestive-tract/symptoms-causes)
catalog_gaps: standalone vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) at a dose under the UL

summary: Ginger supplements may help nausea and vomiting of pregnancy (NCCIH), though evidence is weak for motion sickness, chemotherapy and postoperative nausea. For pregnancy nausea, ACOG (as summarized by ODS) recommends vitamin B6 10-25 mg three or four times daily, adding doxylamine if needed; B6 plus doxylamine reduced nausea and vomiting by about 70% in RCTs. Note: the ACOG FAQ page itself could not be loaded, so ACOG's position is cited via the ODS vitamin B6 fact sheet.

effective_types.type: vitamin B6 + doxylamine (OTC/Rx) for pregnancy nausea
ginger for motion sickness / postoperative / chemotherapy nausea

caution: Ask a clinician before using ginger in pregnancy; breastfeeding safety is not well known; ginger can cause heartburn, abdominal discomfort and diarrhea and may interact with medicines (NCCIH, https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/ginger)
Pregnant women should consult a physician before B6 supplements because doses can approach the 100 mg/day UL (ODS, https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/VitaminB6-HealthProfessional)
see_a_clinician_if: Pregnancy nausea not improving on B6 alone (ACOG advises adding doxylamine under care) (ODS, https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/VitaminB6-HealthProfessional)
Vomiting together with constipation, abdominal pain or inability to pass gas (NIDDK, https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/constipation/symptoms-causes)

summary: NIDDK first-line care is more dietary fiber (22-34 g/day), fluids, activity and bowel routine, then OTC fiber supplements (e.g., psyllium/methylcellulose products), osmotic laxatives (PEG, milk of magnesia), stool softeners, and stimulant laxatives only if severe or other treatments fail; prescription secretagogues and biofeedback follow. Probiotics show some benefit in adults (especially B. lactis) per NCCIH, but evidence is mixed. Note: the AGA/ACG 2023 guideline full text could not be opened (site check), so grades rely on NIDDK and NCCIH.
caution: Drink plenty of fluids when increasing fiber or taking a fiber supplement (NIDDK, https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/constipation/treatment)
Laxatives are generally for short-term use; ask a doctor how to taper long-term use (NIDDK, https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/constipation/treatment)
Guar gum and glucomannan tablets taken without enough fluid have caused esophageal or bowel obstruction (ODS, https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/weightloss-HealthProfessional/)
see_a_clinician_if: Constipation with rectal bleeding, blood in stool, ongoing abdominal pain, inability to pass gas, vomiting, fever, lower back pain or unexplained weight loss (NIDDK, https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/constipation/symptoms-causes)

summary: Probiotics taken with antibiotics roughly halve the risk of antibiotic-associated diarrhea and reduce C. difficile diarrhea (moderate certainty, NCCIH), but strain and dose are uncertain. For IBS with diarrhea, NIDDK lists loperamide and prescription options. No catalog products are matched to this need.

effective_types.type: probiotics during antibiotic courses (antibiotic-associated diarrhea, C. difficile)

caution: Probiotics carry infection risk for severely ill or immunocompromised people (NCCIH, https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/probiotics-usefulness-and-safety)
see_a_clinician_if: Diarrhea with abdominal pain or weight loss, or a sudden change in symptoms (NIDDK, https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/gas-digestive-tract/symptoms-causes)
Fever or blood in stool with bowel changes (NIDDK, https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/constipation/symptoms-causes)
catalog_gaps: single-strain probiotic with antibiotic-associated diarrhea evidence

summary: NIDDK advises swallowing less air, smaller meals, and limiting trigger foods (legumes, cruciferous vegetables, fructose, lactose, sugar alcohols), with lactase products for lactose intolerance and a short low-FODMAP trial for IBS. NCCIH reports a 2020 review where probiotics relieved gas in IBS, while inulin-type prebiotics increased gassiness. ESNM/UEG finds insufficient evidence for simethicone and does not recommend enzyme supplements for functional bloating.
caution: Prebiotic fibers such as inulin can increase gas; doses above 20 g/day can cause gas, bloating and diarrhea (NCCIH, https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/irritable-bowel-syndrome-what-you-need-to-know)
Talk with a doctor before using supplements or probiotics (NIDDK, https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/gas-digestive-tract/treatment)
see_a_clinician_if: Gas with abdominal pain, constipation, diarrhea, weight loss, or a sudden change in symptoms (NIDDK, https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/gas-digestive-tract/symptoms-causes)
catalog_gaps: alpha-galactosidase (not covered by sources reviewed; low priority)

summary: ESNM/UEG (2025) says selected probiotics may improve bloating (low evidence, product-specific), finds insufficient evidence for simethicone or peppermint oil for functional bloating, and does not recommend enzyme supplementation (test for pancreatic insufficiency instead). A low-FODMAP diet improves bloating in IBS in RCTs (StatPearls), and NCCIH notes a 2020 review in which probiotics reduced bloating in IBS. Note: the AGA 2023 bloating clinical practice update could not be opened (site check).

effective_types.type: low-FODMAP diet (IBS bloating, supervised, short term)

caution: Probiotic products differ; results from one cannot be generalized to another (ESNM, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12606050/)
Peppermint oil can worsen reflux; avoid with hernia or GERD (NCCIH, https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/irritable-bowel-syndrome-what-you-need-to-know)
see_a_clinician_if: Bloating with unexplained weight loss, severe or worsening symptoms, or other alarm signs needs evaluation to exclude organic disease such as celiac disease, pancreatic insufficiency, Crohn's, hypothyroidism, diabetes, or GI/gynecologic malignancy (ESNM/UEG consensus, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12606050/)

Gas or bloating that suddenly changes, or comes with abdominal pain, constipation, diarrhea or weight loss (NIDDK, https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/gas-digestive-tract/symptoms-causes)

summary: The 2024 AAD guideline strongly recommends benzoyl peroxide, topical retinoids (adapalene is OTC), topical antibiotics in combination, oral doxycycline and isotretinoin for severe disease, and conditionally recommends combined oral contraceptives and spironolactone for women. AAD's patient pages also list salicylic and azelaic acid. Zinc, diet and supplements are not addressed by the guideline abstract, and AAD advises zinc only for a documented deficiency.
caution: Spironolactone can cause severe birth defects; use birth control while taking it (AAD, https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/acne/derm-treat/treat)
Avoid potassium supplements and coconut water on spironolactone (AAD, https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/acne/derm-treat/hormonal-therapy)
Take zinc only when a blood test shows deficiency (AAD, https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/hair-loss/treatment/diagnosis-treat)
see_a_clinician_if: Severe, nodular or scarring acne, or acne that has not responded to OTC treatment (AAD guideline, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38300170/?dopt=Abstract)

summary: AAD calls topical minoxidil (FDA-approved OTC 2% and 5% for women) the most-recommended treatment for female pattern hair loss, needing 6-12 months of use; spironolactone and other antiandrogen pills are off-label options, and FDA-cleared at-home lasers have some supporting studies. Biotin and folic acid show no effect in most studies, and AAD advises biotin, iron or zinc only for a documented deficiency. Diagnosis matters because postpartum shedding, deficiencies, hormones and hairstyles can all cause hair loss.
caution: Avoid minoxidil if pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding (AAD, https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/hair-loss/types/female-pattern)
Prescription hair-loss pills may cause birth defects (AAD, https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/hair-loss/types/female-pattern)
Excess iron can cause poisoning; supplements can be harmful if levels are normal (AAD, https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/hair-loss/treatment/diagnosis-treat)
see_a_clinician_if: Hair loss that comes on quickly, or may be from disease, deficiency, hormone problems or infection, which may need blood tests or a scalp biopsy (AAD, https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/hair-loss/treatment/diagnosis-treat)

summary: The Endocrine Society guideline (2018) recommends testing for elevated androgens when hirsutism scores are abnormal, combined oral contraceptives as first line for most women not seeking fertility, adding an antiandrogen after 6 months if needed, and photoepilation (laser) or electrolysis for hair removal, with eflornithine cream as an add-on. Lifestyle change is advised for women with obesity and PCOS. No supplements are recommended (Mayo Clinic).
caution: Antiandrogens are teratogenic; use reliable contraception (Endocrine Society, https://www.endocrine.org/clinical-practice-guidelines/hirsutism)

Laser carries higher risk of pigment change in darker skin and paradoxical hypertrichosis in Mediterranean/Middle Eastern women (Endocrine Society, https://www.endocrine.org/clinical-practice-guidelines/hirsutism)
see_a_clinician_if: Heavy or rapid hair growth, or signs of virilization such as a deepening voice, scalp hair loss, increased muscle mass or enlarged clitoris (Mayo Clinic, https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/hirsutism/symptoms-causes/syc-20354935)
Irregular periods or progression despite therapy (Endocrine Society, https://www.endocrine.org/clinical-practice-guidelines/hirsutism)
catalog_gaps: at-home hair-removal tools (types only; device-specific evidence not reviewed)
telehealth access to OCP/antiandrogen prescribing for hirsutism

summary: For adult women with persistent acne on the jawline, lower face or neck, AAD supports hormonal therapy: combined oral contraceptives (2-3 months to work) and spironolactone (50-100% reduction in studies), both conditionally recommended in the 2024 AAD guideline. These are prescription treatments, so access through a clinician or telehealth is the evidence-backed path. No supplement is recommended.
caution: Spironolactone requires contraception and blood tests; avoid potassium supplements (AAD, https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/acne/derm-treat/hormonal-therapy)
OCPs raise clot, heart attack and blood pressure risks; screened before prescribing (AAD, https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/acne/derm-treat/hormonal-therapy)
see_a_clinician_if: Acne with excess hair, irregular periods or other signs of androgen excess, which may signal PCOS (Endocrine Society, https://www.endocrine.org/patient-engagement/endocrine-library/hirsutism)

summary: ODS concludes that no weight-loss supplement has strong evidence of meaningful, lasting weight loss; lifestyle change (diet, calorie reduction, physical activity) is the basis. Caffeine and green tea may have small, short-term effects; chromium has a minimal effect (about 1.1 kg); garcinia, glucomannan, guar gum and probiotics show little or inconsistent effect. Several ingredients carry real harms.
caution: Green tea extract linked to liver damage; garcinia to liver toxicity and mania; yohimbe to heart attack and death (ODS, https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/weightloss-HealthProfessional/)
People with high blood pressure, diabetes, or liver or heart disease should consult a provider first (ODS, https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/weightloss-HealthProfessional/)
see_a_clinician_if: Unexplained weight loss with digestive symptoms (NIDDK, https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/gas-digestive-tract/symptoms-causes)
Weight concerns with hirsutism or irregular periods (possible PCOS) (Endocrine Society, https://www.endocrine.org/patient-engagement/endocrine-library/hirsutism)

summary: Creatine monohydrate is one of the most studied supplements: it increases strength and power in both men and women and, with resistance training, gives greater gains in strength and muscle size (ODS, Mayo Clinic). Common dosing is 3-5 g/day maintenance (with or without a 20 g/day loading week). Resistance training is the base; wearables and sleep devices do not build strength themselves. Note: ISSN position stand and women-specific meta-analyses on PMC could not be opened (site check).

effective_types.type: creatine monohydrate 3-5 g/day with resistance training

caution: Expect 1-2 kg water-weight gain; anecdotal nausea, diarrhea, cramps (ODS, https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/ExerciseAndAthleticPerformance-HealthProfessional)
People with kidney disease should talk with their care team before creatine (Mayo Clinic, https://www.mayoclinic.org/drugs-supplements-creatine/art-20347591)
see_a_clinician_if: Existing kidney disease before starting creatine (Mayo Clinic, https://www.mayoclinic.org/drugs-supplements-creatine/art-20347591)

summary: No pregnancy-specific bloating treatment was found in the reviewed sources. Pregnancy commonly causes constipation (NIDDK), so fluids, dietary fiber and activity are reasonable first steps, but supplements in pregnancy should be cleared with a clinician (NCCIH). No catalog products are matched to this need.

effective_types.type: dietary fiber, fluids, activity (pregnancy constipation-related bloating)

caution: Discuss any non-vitamin/mineral supplement in pregnancy with a provider (NCCIH, https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/womens-health-and-complementary-approaches?nav=govd)
Lactase products may not be suitable for pregnant or breastfeeding women without medical advice (NIDDK, https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/lactose-intolerance/treatment)
see_a_clinician_if: Bloating with vomiting, fever, ongoing abdominal pain, bleeding or inability to pass gas (NIDDK, https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/constipation/symptoms-causes)

summary: Bloating has many causes; ESNM/UEG recommends ruling out organic disease, then considering diet (low-FODMAP in IBS), selected probiotics (low evidence), and brain-gut therapies, and does not recommend enzyme blends or simethicone. Constipation-related bloating responds to constipation treatment such as fiber and osmotic laxatives (NIDDK).
caution: Probiotics carry infection risk for the severely ill or immunocompromised (NCCIH, https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/probiotics-usefulness-and-safety)
see_a_clinician_if: Bloating with unexplained weight loss, severe or worsening symptoms, or other alarm signs needs evaluation to exclude organic disease such as celiac disease, pancreatic insufficiency, Crohn's, hypothyroidism, diabetes, or GI/gynecologic malignancy (ESNM/UEG consensus, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12606050/)

Gas or bloating that suddenly changes, or comes with abdominal pain, constipation, diarrhea or weight loss (NIDDK, https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/gas-digestive-tract/symptoms-causes)

summary: Urine LH tests accurately detect the LH surge that precedes ovulation by about 1-1.5 days (ASRM, FDA; FDA cites ~9 in 10 reliability with correct use); ovulation can still occur up to 2 days after the surge and ~7% of cycles give false positives. BBT and PdG/progesterone only confirm ovulation after the fact. Cervical mucus is a cheap, valid marker. Calendar-based apps predicted ovulation day at most 21% of the time in one study (ASRM). Saliva ferning tests are unreliable (FDA).

effective_types.type: urine LH ovulation test (strips or digital reader)
basal body temperature charting / temperature-based algorithm (confirms, does not predict)
urine PdG (progesterone metabolite) test to confirm ovulation

caution: LH and saliva ovulation tests must not be used to prevent pregnancy (FDA https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/home-use-tests/ovulation-urine-test)
Natural Cycles is not for people on hormonal birth control or for whom pregnancy would be high-risk (FDA https://www.fda.gov/NewsEvents/Newsroom/PressAnnouncements/ucm616511.htm)
see_a_clinician_if: no LH surge detected in 2 or more consecutive cycles, suggesting an ovulation problem (ASRM https://integration.reproductivefacts.org/globalassets/_rf/news-and-publications/bookletsfact-sheets/english-pdf/ovulation_detection_factsheet.pdf)
irregular cycles (ASRM https://integration.reproductivefacts.org/globalassets/_rf/news-and-publications/bookletsfact-sheets/english-pdf/ovulation_detection_factsheet.pdf)
catalog_gaps: plain urine LH test strips (low-cost, no reader)

summary: Cochrane (2023) found timed intercourse using urine LH tests probably increases live birth (RR 1.36) and pregnancy (RR 1.28) versus no ovulation prediction (moderate certainty, women under 40 trying under 12 months; many studies industry-funded). ASRM advises intercourse every 1-2 days in the 6-day fertile window, not limiting frequency, at least 400 mcg folic acid daily, avoiding smoking and heavy alcohol, and keeping caffeine to 1-2 cups. Antioxidants and herbal remedies have little evidence in women without ovulatory dysfunction.

effective_types.type: regular intercourse every 1-2 days in the fertile window
fertility-awareness methods (BBT, mucus, apps) for timing

caution: over-strict timing can add stress and reduce intercourse; use tracking to guide, not replace, regular sex (ASRM https://integration.asrm.org/globalassets/_asrm/practice-guidance/practice-guidelines/pdf/optimizing_natural_fertility.pdf)

some water-based lubricants, olive oil and saliva reduce sperm motility in vitro; mineral oil, canola oil or hydroxyethylcellulose-based lubricants did not (ASRM https://www.asrm.org/practice-guidance/practice-committee-documents/optimizing-natural-fertility-a-committee-opinion-2021)
see_a_clinician_if: no pregnancy after 12 months of regular unprotected sex if under 35 (ASRM https://www.asrm.org/practice-guidance/practice-committee-documents/optimizing-natural-fertility-a-committee-opinion-2021)
no pregnancy after 6 months if 35 or older (ASRM https://www.asrm.org/practice-guidance/practice-committee-documents/optimizing-natural-fertility-a-committee-opinion-2021)
catalog_gaps: folic acid 400 mcg supplement (folic acid form)

summary: Evidence-based fertility support is mostly lifestyle (no smoking, limited alcohol/caffeine, healthy weight), folic acid, accurate fertile-window timing, and timely evaluation by a specialist (after 12 months, or 6 if 35+) (ASRM). Cochrane (2020) found antioxidants may raise clinical pregnancy (CoQ10 among those helping) but the evidence is low quality and mostly in subfertile/IVF populations. Luteal progesterone support in IUI/intercourse cycles has very low to low certainty evidence and no trials of topical OTC progesterone or of natural cycles (Cochrane 2022).

effective_types.type: OTC topical progesterone or herbal blends (vitex, ashwagandha, maca)

caution: Cochrane authors advise taking antioxidants other than prenatal-style combinations only on medical advice, especially with PCOS (https://www.cochrane.org/podcasts/10.1002/14651858.CD007807.pub4)
see_a_clinician_if: 12 months trying under 35, 6 months at 35+ (ASRM https://www.asrm.org/practice-guidance/practice-committee-documents/optimizing-natural-fertility-a-committee-opinion-2021)
irregular cycles or no detected ovulation (ASRM https://integration.reproductivefacts.org/globalassets/_rf/news-and-publications/bookletsfact-sheets/english-pdf/ovulation_detection_factsheet.pdf)
catalog_gaps: at-home semen analysis is present only inside a bundle; standalone FDA-cleared male fertility test

summary: Folic acid 400 mcg daily for anyone who could become pregnant, started before conception, cuts neural tube defects by about 70% (Cochrane 2015, high certainty). CDC states folic acid is the only folate form proven in RCTs to prevent NTDs; 5-MTHF (methylfolate) effectiveness and dose are unknown, and MTHFR variants do not require methylfolate. Folic acid in later pregnancy reduces megaloblastic anaemia (Cochrane 2021).

effective_types.type: prenatal vitamin with folic acid 400 mcg (folic acid form)
prenatal care / telehealth access to clinicians

caution: check the label: 'folate' does not mean folic acid; the folic acid amount is shown in parentheses on updated labels (CDC https://www.cdc.gov/folic-acid/media/pdfs/cdc-presentation-folic-acid-best-tool-prevent-ntds-p.pdf)

higher doses (1,000-4,000 mcg) only on clinician advice, e.g. prior NTD pregnancy or certain antiseizure drugs (CDC https://www.cdc.gov/folic-acid/media/pdfs/cdc-presentation-folic-acid-best-tool-prevent-ntds-p.pdf)
see_a_clinician_if: prior NTD-affected pregnancy, family history of NTDs, or antiseizure medication use (CDC https://www.cdc.gov/folic-acid/media/pdfs/cdc-presentation-folic-acid-best-tool-prevent-ntds-p.pdf)
catalog_gaps: prenatal vitamin that uses folic acid (not only methylfolate)

summary: Pregnancy-safe discovery is about whether a product is appropriate to use while pregnant, not whether it treats anything. External items (pillows, belts, plain emollients) are low-risk by nature; ingested products need label checks (e.g. folic acid form per CDC). Ingredient-level pregnancy safety for topicals (e.g. retinyl palmitate) could not be verified this session: credible-source pages for this need (NCBI/PubMed/PMC/LactMed, ACOG, Mayo, NHS, ODS, NCCIH) were blocked or unreachable this session, so evidence is unverified.
caution: home pregnancy test negatives are tentative; avoid medicines and harmful exposures until pregnancy is ruled out (FDA https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/home-use-tests/pregnancy)

summary: FDA: breast pumps are regulated medical devices that help maintain or increase milk supply, relieve engorgement and plugged ducts, and draw out flat or inverted nipples. Battery/electric and double pumps are faster for work or frequent pumping, and manual pumps make a good backup. Shield fit matters, and pumping should not hurt or bleed. Nipple-care products, nursing pads and pillows could not be verified this session (credible-source pages for this need (NCBI/PubMed/PMC/LactMed, ACOG, Mayo, NHS, ODS, NCCIH) were blocked or unreachable this session, so evidence is unverified).

effective_types.type: electric/battery breast pump (double for frequent pumping)
nipple balms, silver cups, nursing pads, nursing pillows

caution: never buy a used single-user pump; only multi-user pumps can be rented or shared, and each user needs their own accessory kit (FDA https://www.fda.gov/consumers/consumer-updates/what-know-when-buying-or-using-breast-pump)

soreness, yellowish discharge, fever or flu-like symptoms not improving in 24-48 hours (FDA https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/breast-pumps/injury-and-infection)

Products with retinoids (retinyl palmitate) need a pregnancy/breastfeeding ingredient check.

summary: For pregnancy back and pelvic pain, exercise (land or water based, 8 to 12 weeks) reduces pain and sick leave with low to moderate certainty, and acupuncture helped pelvic pain in single trials (Cochrane 2015). NHS advice adds a supportive mattress, back support when sitting (maternity support pillows), paracetamol, and physiotherapy referral for severe pain; a pelvic support belt may help pelvic girdle pain after physio advice. In the third trimester, side sleeping with pillows between the knees, under the bump and behind the back is advised. Moisturizers can ease itchy, dry pregnancy skin.

effective_types.type: acupuncture for pelvic girdle pain (clinician delivered)
maternity support pillow / pillows for side sleeping
emollient creams or lotions for itchy, dry skin

caution: Avoid retinoid skin products (tretinoin, tazarotene, OTC retinol) in pregnancy (AAD; NHS)
Ask a physiotherapist before using a pelvic support belt, as it may not suit everyone (St George's NHS leaflet)
Avoid exercises lying flat on the back in the second and third trimester, contact sports and hot yoga (MotherToBaby via NCBI Bookshelf)
see_a_clinician_if: Back pain in the second or third trimester (possible early labour), or with fever, vaginal bleeding or pain when peeing; call 911 if you lose feeling in your legs, bottom or genitals (NHS)
Severe itching without a rash, especially on palms and soles, in the second or third trimester (possible cholestasis of pregnancy) (AAFP)
Pain under the ribs, severe headache, or vision changes (possible preeclampsia) (NHS; Mayo Clinic)
catalog_gaps: prenatal exercise class or program (aquanatal, prenatal yoga)

summary: Ice packs or cold gel pads may reduce perineal pain in the first hours to two days after birth (Cochrane 2020, very low to low certainty), usually alongside OTC or prescription pain relief. NICE advises daily showering of the perineum, frequent pad changes, discussing pain relief that fits breastfeeding, and discussing pelvic floor exercises at every postnatal contact. Antenatal pelvic floor muscle training prevents urinary incontinence in continent women into the postnatal period (high to moderate certainty), while evidence for PFMT started after birth or for treating established incontinence is weaker. Prolapse is managed with supervised pelvic floor exercises, a pessary or surgery; diastasis recti with PT-guided deep core work.

effective_types.type: perineal cooling (ice pack or cold gel pad, 10 to 20 min, first 48 h)
pelvic floor muscle training (antenatal and postnatal)
perineal hygiene (daily shower, frequent pad changes)

caution: Cooling likely needs to be combined with pain relief, and harms were poorly reported in trials (Cochrane CD006304)
Pick pain relief that fits breastfeeding (NICE NG194 1.2.19)
With diastasis recti avoid crunches, sit-ups and unmodified planks, and lift nothing heavier than the baby for six weeks (Cleveland Clinic)
Belly binders do not heal diastasis recti; they only support posture (Cleveland Clinic)
see_a_clinician_if: Perineal pain that is not resolving or is worsening, smelly discharge, swelling, or wound breakdown (same-day referral if the wound has broken down) (NICE NG194)
Heavy bleeding (soaking a pad an hour), clots bigger than an egg, fever 100.4F or higher, severe headache, or thoughts of harming yourself or the baby (CDC Hear Her)
Abdominal muscle gap wider than two finger widths or pain (Cleveland Clinic)
catalog_gaps: OTC pain relief suitable for breastfeeding (acetaminophen, ibuprofen)
plain perineal cold gel pad or ice pack (already partly covered)

summary: Cochrane found no high-quality evidence that any topical cream or oil prevents stretch marks (5 trials, RR 0.74, not significant, low certainty), and NHS says there is very little evidence such products work. AAFP notes Centella asiatica or hyaluronic acid with daily massage may give a modest preventive benefit, and that topical tretinoin, laser and microneedling are postpartum treatment options. Retinoid creams should not be used during pregnancy; plain moisturizers keep skin comfortable.

effective_types.type: Centella asiatica or hyaluronic acid topical with massage (prevention)
prescription tretinoin, laser or microneedling (postpartum treatment, clinician led)
OTC oils and butters (olive, cocoa, almond) for prevention

caution: Retinoid creams should not be used during pregnancy (NHS; AAD); ask a clinician about retinoids while breastfeeding (AAD)
Stretch marks usually fade but may not disappear; no product reliably removes them (NHS; AAFP familydoctor.org)
see_a_clinician_if: A rash, spots or markings that concern you, or severe itching (AAFP familydoctor.org)
catalog_gaps: Centella asiatica or hyaluronic acid stretch-mark topical
dermatology telehealth for postpartum stretch-mark treatment

summary: (Pass 2 covers nipple care and nursing accessories only.) The main fix for nipple pain is correcting positioning and latch with a midwife, lactation consultant or peer supporter (NHS; NICE NG194 1.5.15). Cochrane found insufficient evidence that any topical treatment (lanolin, gel pads, breast milk, ointments) beats applying nothing (low certainty), though LactMed concludes purified lanolin appears effective and similar to breast milk, hydrogel and other options. NHS advises changing breast pads after every feed, letting nipples dry, and avoiding breast shells and nipple shields.

effective_types.type: latch and positioning help (lactation consultant, midwife, peer support)
breast (nursing) pads for leaks, changed every feed

caution: Avoid lanolin with a known wool allergy (LactMed)
NHS advises against breast shells and nipple shields for sore nipples, as they do not fix attachment (NHS)
Never let a baby sleep on a nursing pillow or other soft surface; sleep surfaces must be firm and flat (NICHD Safe to Sleep)
see_a_clinician_if: Cracked or bleeding nipples (higher infection risk, including thrush) (NHS)
Breast redness and swelling worsening or lasting more than 24 hours despite self-care (possible mastitis) (NICE NG194)
Fever of 100.4F or higher (CDC Hear Her)

summary: Hormone therapy is the most effective treatment. FDA-approved nonhormone options are low-dose paroxetine and fezolinetant (elinzanetant is also FDA-approved per Mayo), with SSRIs/SNRIs, gabapentin and oxybutynin used off-label. The Menopause Society 2023 nonhormone position statement recommends CBT, clinical hypnosis and weight loss. It does NOT recommend paced respiration, supplements/herbal remedies, cooling techniques, exercise, yoga, soy products or acupuncture, because evidence is limited or negative. Cochrane reviews find no conclusive benefit from black cohosh or phytoestrogens over placebo.

effective_types.type: prescription hormone therapy (via clinician or telehealth)
cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for hot flashes
cooling techniques (fans, layers, cold drinks, cooling products)

caution: Black cohosh: rare reports of liver injury; stop if dark urine, jaundice or abdominal pain; people with liver disorders should ask a clinician first (NCCIH https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/menopausal-symptoms-in-depth; ODS)

Soy/isoflavones may act like estrogen; people with a history of breast cancer should check with a clinician before isoflavone pills (Mayo https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/menopause/diagnosis-treatment/drc-20353401)
Herbal supplements can interact with medicines and product contents vary (NICE https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng23/chapter/recommendations)
Discuss antidepressants for hot flashes with your clinician if you have a history of breast cancer (The Menopause Society https://menopause.org/patient-education/menopause-topics/hot-flashes)
see_a_clinician_if: Hot flashes remain significantly disruptive despite lifestyle approaches (The Menopause Society hot flashes page)
You have or are at risk for breast or endometrial cancer, heart disease, stroke or blood clots and are considering estrogen (Mayo Clinic hot flashes)
Symptoms start before 45, or before 40 (possible premature ovarian insufficiency) (NICE NG23)
catalog_gaps: CBT program for menopausal hot flashes (digital or therapist-led)
clinical hypnosis program for hot flashes
telehealth prescribing of fezolinetant / nonhormone Rx (verify catalog telehealth services cover this)

summary: Night sweats are vasomotor symptoms and respond to the same treatments as hot flashes: hormone therapy is most effective, and CBT, hypnosis, fezolinetant, SSRIs/SNRIs and gabapentin are evidence-based options. Mayo suggests keeping the bedroom cool, using fans and cold packs under the pillow, but The Menopause Society 2023 does not recommend cooling techniques as treatment because evidence is limited. They are low-risk comfort measures, not proven therapy. NCCIH reports hypnotherapy improved sleep and hot-flash interference in an NIH-funded trial.

effective_types.type: cool bedroom / fans / cold packs / cooling bedding

caution: Same supplement cautions as hot flashes: black cohosh liver reports (ODS https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/BlackCohosh-HealthProfessional/), isoflavones and breast cancer history (Mayo menopause)
see_a_clinician_if: Night sweats are significantly disrupting sleep despite lifestyle measures (The Menopause Society hot flashes page)
Sweats occur outside the menopause transition or with other symptoms, since other conditions such as an overactive thyroid can mimic menopause (Mayo Clinic menopause)
catalog_gaps: CBT program targeting menopausal night sweats and insomnia

summary: Menopause body changes covered here include vaginal dryness (genitourinary syndrome of menopause), bone loss, vasomotor symptoms and mood. For vaginal dryness, The Menopause Society and NICE name OTC vaginal moisturizers (used regularly) and lubricants (for sex) as first-line options. Evidence for specific OTC products is limited, and in one 12-week RCT moisturizer, low-dose vaginal estradiol and placebo gel helped similarly. Low-dose vaginal estrogen is effective and safe. Avoid glycerin, parabens, warming or flavored products, and natural oils like coconut or olive oil (linked to vaginal infections). Clinician-led care, including telehealth, gives access to hormone therapy and Rx options. Most herbal menopause supplements lack evidence.

effective_types.type: low-dose vaginal estrogen / vaginal DHEA (Rx) for vaginal dryness
OTC vaginal moisturizer (water-based, hyaluronic acid or polycarbophil), regular use
water- or silicone-based lubricant for sex
menopause-focused clinician care / telehealth with HT prescribing
symptom log / tracker to bring to visits
CBT for menopause-related low mood or anxiety
home hormone (FSH) tests to diagnose menopause
herbal menopause supplements (black cohosh, soy, ashwagandha)

caution: Oil-based lubricants can weaken latex condoms and may raise vaginal infection risk (The Menopause Society MenoNote GSM https://menopause.org/wp-content/uploads/for-women/MenoNote-GSM.pdf)

Avoid vaginal products with glycerin, parabens, warming agents, flavorings or spermicides, which can irritate tissue (NAMS/ISSWSH consensus https://menopause.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Management_of_genitourinary_syndrome_of_menopause.97565-2.pdf)
Lubricant osmolality ideally under 380 mOsm/kg (WHO) and pH about 3.8-4.5; most products do not list osmolality (NAMS/ISSWSH consensus)
Ashwagandha: avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding, not for thyroid disorders, rare liver injury (NCCIH https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/ashwagandha)
Compounded vaginal estrogen or testosterone is not regulated or recommended for GSM (The Menopause Society MenoNote GSM)
see_a_clinician_if: Vaginal symptoms do not improve with OTC products, since yeast infections, allergic reactions and skin conditions can look similar (The Menopause Society MenoNote GSM)
Treatments do not improve symptoms or cause ongoing side effects, or there are contraindications to HRT (NICE NG23 referral criteria)
Under 45 with menopausal symptoms, or under 40 with suspected premature ovarian insufficiency (NICE NG23)
catalog_gaps: telehealth or clinician pathway to low-dose vaginal estrogen (verify catalog telehealth services cover it)
pelvic/vulvar care product with published osmolality (types only)

summary: Women 51+ need 1,200 mg calcium and 600 IU vitamin D a day (800 IU over 70), ideally from food plus supplements if needed (ODS). Calcium plus vitamin D modestly raises bone density in some postmenopausal women, but fracture evidence is mixed. USPSTF found moderate certainty that 1,000 mg or less of calcium with 400 IU or less of vitamin D does not prevent fractures in postmenopausal women, and VITAL found 2,000 IU D3 alone did not cut fractures. Calcium citrate absorbs without food and is absorbed best in doses of 500 mg or less. Regular exercise, balance work (yoga, tai chi) and, when indicated, hormone therapy or osteoporosis medicines protect bone.

effective_types.type: calcium (to reach 1,200 mg/day total) + vitamin D (600-800 IU/day) to meet intake
low-dose calcium+D supplement for fracture prevention in community-dwelling postmenopausal women
weight-bearing and balance exercise (yoga, tai chi)

caution: Do not exceed calcium UL of 2,000 mg/day (age 51+); supplemental calcium has mixed evidence on kidney stones and cardiovascular risk (ODS https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Calcium-HealthProfessional/%23h3)
Vitamin D UL is 4,000 IU/day; high calcium plus vitamin D raised kidney stone risk 17% in WHI (ODS https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/VitaminD-HealthProfessional/)
Vitamin D interacts with orlistat, statins, steroids and thiazide diuretics (ODS vitamin D)
see_a_clinician_if: You are an older adult unsure of your calcium/vitamin D needs (ODS vitamin D)
At menopause review, ask about bone health and fragility fracture risk assessment (NICE NG23)
catalog_gaps: clinician pathway for bone density and fracture-risk assessment

summary: PMDD is a recognized depressive disorder tied to the menstrual cycle and is treatable; NIMH advises starting with a primary care provider or ob-gyn for evaluation and referral. Clinician-led care (psychotherapy, medication) is the core option. Among supplements, vitamin B6 (up to 100 mg/day) has a low-quality systematic review suggesting benefit for premenstrual symptoms including depressive symptoms; chasteberry evidence covers physical PMS symptoms, not mood. (The ACOG 2023 premenstrual disorders guideline could not be retrieved in this session.)

effective_types.type: clinician evaluation and treatment (in person or telehealth)
internet or app-based CBT (indirect, from anxiety evidence)

caution: Chasteberry may be unsafe in pregnancy and breastfeeding and in hormone-sensitive cancers (https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/chasteberry)

summary: Fatigue is a classic symptom of iron deficiency anemia; women of reproductive age and those with heavy periods are at high risk, and serum ferritin is the most efficient test (under 30 mcg/L suggests deficiency). Iron should be taken when deficiency is shown or a clinician recommends it, not as a blind energy booster. A meta-analysis of 13 RCTs found CoQ10 reduced fatigue mainly in people with disease, not significantly in healthy people; B vitamins and creatine lack evidence for general fatigue.

effective_types.type: ferritin test, then iron only if deficient

caution: Iron: UL 45 mg/day; avoid with hemochromatosis; interacts with levothyroxine and levodopa; keep away from children (https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Iron-HealthProfessional/)
Creatine: LactMed suggests avoiding while breastfeeding (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sites/books/NBK501853/)
see_a_clinician_if: Fatigue with heavy menstrual bleeding, weakness or difficulty concentrating (possible iron deficiency anemia) (https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Iron-HealthProfessional/)
Dark urine or fatigue while taking black cohosh or other herbals (possible liver injury) (https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/black-cohosh)
catalog_gaps: at-home or lab ferritin / iron panel test

summary: The AASM strongly recommends multicomponent CBT-I for chronic insomnia and conditionally recommends brief behavioral therapy and relaxation therapy; sleep hygiene alone is conditionally not recommended and no recommendation was made on mindfulness or on specific delivery methods (internet programs can be discussed). Melatonin is not recommended for chronic insomnia (AASM 2017) though it helps jet lag; magnesium has three small low-quality trials (about 17 minutes faster sleep onset in older adults). Ashwagandha may help some with insomnia but has liver and thyroid cautions.

effective_types.type: sleep hygiene alone; cool, dark, quiet bedroom

caution: Melatonin: limited pregnancy data, ask a clinician; occasional evening doses unlikely to harm a breastfed infant; gummies often mislabeled (74-347% of label); keep from children (https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/melatonin-what-you-need-to-know; https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501863/)
Ashwagandha: avoid in pregnancy/breastfeeding and thyroid disease; rare liver injury (https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/ashwagandha)
Magnesium supplements above 350 mg/day cause diarrhea and cramping; higher toxicity risk with kidney disease (https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Magnesium-HealthProfessional/)
see_a_clinician_if: Insomnia lasting months or affecting daytime function (chronic insomnia warrants CBT-I) (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7853203/)
Daytime sleepiness in older adults on melatonin (https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/melatonin-what-you-need-to-know)
catalog_gaps: melatonin (for jet lag / circadian timing only)

summary: No credible source defines a proven product for 'brain fog'. Iron deficiency anemia causes difficulty concentrating, and poor sleep impairs problem-solving, so testing for deficiency and treating sleep are the evidence-backed first steps. Ginkgo's effect on cognition in healthy people is uncertain and large trials found no dementia prevention; short-term B vitamins showed no cognitive benefit in adults over 50.

effective_types.type: ferritin test and iron if deficient

caution: Ginkgo may increase bleeding with anticoagulants and may be unsafe in pregnancy (https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/ginkgo)
see_a_clinician_if: New or worsening memory or concentration problems, especially with fatigue or heavy periods (https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Iron-HealthProfessional/)

summary: Difficulty concentrating is listed by ODS as a symptom of iron deficiency anemia and by ACOG as a PMS-like symptom worsened by poor sleep. Evidence-backed steps are checking for deficiency and fixing sleep; supplements marketed for focus (ginkgo, B vitamins) lack good evidence in healthy adults.

effective_types.type: ferritin test and iron if deficient

caution: Chronic high-dose vitamin B6 can cause sensory neuropathy (https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/providers/digest/dietary-supplements-and-cognitive-function-dementia-and-alzheimers-disease-science)
see_a_clinician_if: Concentration problems with fatigue, weakness or heavy menstrual bleeding (https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Iron-HealthProfessional/)

summary: First-line self-care for period cramps per NHS and Mayo is heat on the lower abdomen (heat pad, hot water bottle, heat patch, warm bath), OTC NSAIDs such as ibuprofen or naproxen started the day before the period, and regular exercise; hormonal contraception is the next step via a clinician. Cochrane (2024) finds high- and low-frequency TENS may reduce pain vs placebo (low certainty), and Cochrane (2019) finds exercise about 45-60 min 3x/week may cut pain ~25 mm on a 100 mm scale (low certainty). Cochrane (2016) finds no high-quality evidence for any dietary supplement; fish oil, ginger, vitamin B1, zinc and fenugreek have only very limited low-quality evidence and vitamin E showed none.

effective_types.type: heat therapy (heat pad, wrap, hot water bottle)

caution: Do not use TENS in pregnancy unless a doctor or midwife says to, or with epilepsy or a pacemaker; do not use on broken or numb skin (NHS TENS: https://www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/transcutaneous-electrical-nerve-stimulation-tens/)
Wrap hot water bottles/heat pads in a cloth rather than on bare skin (NHS: https://www.nhs.uk/symptoms/period-pain/)
Supplement safety evidence is lacking for period pain; few trials reported adverse effects (Cochrane: https://cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD002124.pub2)
see_a_clinician_if: Pain stops usual daily activities, or periods become more painful, heavier or irregular (NHS)
Severe pain or pain worse than usual that painkillers have not helped: urgent appointment (NHS)
Pain during sex, pain when peeing or pooing, bleeding between periods, swollen tummy or unexplained weight loss (NHS)
Cramps disrupt life every month, are steadily worsening, or severe cramps start after age 25 (Mayo)
Possible endometriosis, adenomyosis, fibroids, PID, or a new IUD as the cause (NHS, Mayo)

summary: Pelvic pain has many causes (gynecologic, bowel, urinary, musculoskeletal, pelvic floor dysfunction), so NHS says not to self-diagnose and treatment depends on the cause. Cleveland Clinic lists OTC pain relievers, a heating pad or warm compress, warm baths, gentle stretching, exercise and physical therapy for home care; NHS lists physiotherapy including pelvic floor exercises among GP options. Endometriosis commonly presents as pelvic pain plus painful periods, pain with sex or bowel movements, and can take a long time to diagnose.

effective_types.type: pelvic trigger point wand (self-release under PT guidance)

caution: Pelvic pain in pregnancy needs a pregnancy care provider if it does not ease with rest or position change; pregnancy-related pelvic girdle pain is managed with physiotherapy (Cleveland Clinic: https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/symptoms/12106-pelvic-pain; NHS: https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/common-symptoms/pelvic-pain/)
Self-treatment with heat or devices should not delay diagnosis of the cause (NHS: https://www.nhs.uk/symptoms/pelvic-pain/)
see_a_clinician_if: Call emergency services: severe or worsening pain, pain on movement or touch, fainting/dizziness, shoulder-tip pain, difficulty breathing, heavy vaginal bleeding, sudden confusion (NHS)
Urgent advice: pain with difficulty or pain peeing/pooing, blood in urine or stool, unusual discharge or bleeding, high temperature, vomiting and diarrhoea, or possible pregnancy (NHS)
Sharp, sudden pain not improving with rest or pain relief; heavy bleeding filling a pad every hour for several hours; fever with vomiting (Cleveland Clinic)
Pain lasting more than a few days, recurring, or interfering with daily life; persistent bloating, early fullness, or unintended weight loss (Cleveland Clinic, NHS)
Symptoms suggesting endometriosis: pain during/after sex, pain when pooing or peeing, difficulty getting pregnant, symptoms affecting daily life (NHS endometriosis)

summary: For painful sex linked to dryness, ACOG, Mayo, Cleveland Clinic and The Menopause Society all name water- or silicone-based lubricants before sex and regular vaginal moisturizers (every few days) as first-line nonprescription options; avoid oil-based lubricants (irritation, condom failure) and products with fragrance, flavors, warming/cooling agents, glycerin, propylene glycol or parabens. Vaginal dilators and pelvic floor physical therapy are recommended for vaginismus, vulvodynia, vaginal narrowing and pelvic floor tension, ideally with PT or specialist guidance; Cochrane found the trial evidence for systematic desensitisation in vaginismus too limited to confirm benefit, while Cleveland Clinic cites ~80% response to multi-component treatment. Prescription vaginal estrogen or ospemifene treat menopause-related dyspareunia.

Avoid lubricants with glycerin, warming (capsaicin) or cooling ingredients, fragrance, flavors, propylene glycol, parabens when tissue is sensitive (Mayo: https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/vaginal-atrophy/diagnosis-treatment/drc-20352294; Mayo vulvodynia: https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/vulvodynia/diagnosis-treatment/drc-20353427; NAMS: https://menopause.org/wp-content/uploads/for-women/MenoNote-GSM.pdf)

summary: Pads, liners, tampons, menstrual cups/discs and period underwear are all FDA-regulated medical devices and established ways to manage periods; the best choice is personal preference. Cups (silicone, up to 12 h) leak about as often as or less often than tampons (Cleveland Clinic). Discs are grouped with cups by FDA but have less disc-specific evidence. Organic cotton has no proven safety advantage, since FDA says modern bleaching keeps dioxin below harmful levels.

caution: Tampons: never more than 8 h; use the lowest absorbency that works; people who have had TSS should avoid tampons (Mayo Clinic, https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/toxic-shock-syndrome/symptoms-causes/syc-20355384; FDA, https://www.fda.gov/forconsumers/consumerupdates/ucm612029.htm)

Cups and discs: TSS is possible if they are left in too long; empty within 12 h (Cleveland Clinic, https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/15437-toxic-shock-syndrome; FDA, https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/menstrual-product-options-facts-and-safe-use/menstrual-cups)

Cups/discs with an IUD: they can dislodge IUD strings or placement, so check with a gynecologist first (FDA, https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/menstrual-product-options-facts-and-safe-use/menstrual-cups; Cleveland Clinic, https://health.clevelandclinic.org/menstrual-cup)
Latex allergy: choose silicone, not rubber, cups (FDA, https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/menstrual-product-options-facts-and-safe-use/menstrual-cups)
Scented or essential-oil pads can irritate vulvar skin; prefer unscented (Cleveland Clinic, https://health.clevelandclinic.org/sanitary-pads)
Prolapse or a low uterus may stop a cup sitting properly (Cleveland Clinic, https://health.clevelandclinic.org/menstrual-cup)
Tampons and cups are for menstrual bleeding only, not postpartum or other bleeding (FDA, https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/menstrual-product-options-facts-and-safe-use/menstrual-cups)
see_a_clinician_if: Sudden fever (around 102F or higher), vomiting, diarrhea, dizziness or fainting, or a sunburn-like rash during or just after a period while using a tampon/cup/disc: remove it and seek urgent care (FDA, https://www.fda.gov/forconsumers/consumerupdates/ucm612029.htm; NHS, https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/toxic-shock-syndrome/)
Itching, rash, pain or swelling from any product (FDA, https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/menstrual-product-options-facts-and-safe-use/menstrual-pads-and-liners)
Pain when inserting a cup (Cleveland Clinic, https://health.clevelandclinic.org/menstrual-cup)

summary: Heavy menstrual bleeding (changing a pad or tampon in under 2 hours, soaking through hourly, doubling up, quarter-size clots, more than 7 days) needs medical evaluation, including a full blood count and, where relevant, bleeding-disorder testing (NICE, CDC, ACOG via AAFP). First-line treatments are the LNG-IUS, then tranexamic acid, NSAIDs or hormonal options, plus iron for deficiency. High-capacity products (cups, discs, super/overnight pads, period underwear plus backup) only manage flow and should be paired with getting care.

oral iron for iron deficiency (60-120 mg/day elemental in adolescents)
period tracking (dates plus pads/tampons used) to bring to the visit
high-capacity collection products (larger cup, disc, overnight/super pads) to manage flow

Periods longer than 7 days, clots larger than a quarter, or needing to double up or change overnight (CDC, https://www.cdc.gov/female-blood-disorders/about/heavy-menstrual-bleeding.html)

Bleeding between periods, after sex or after menopause (Mayo Clinic, https://mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/menorrhagia/symptoms-causes/syc-20352829; NHS, https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/periods/)
Dizziness, fainting or bleeding through clothes: urgent care (AAFP, https://www.aafp.org/afp/2020/0515/p633)

period/flow tracker app or pictorial blood-loss chart

caution: Don't use a higher-absorbency tampon than needed; if a tampon lasts 8 h without changing, the absorbency may be too high (FDA, https://www.fda.gov/forconsumers/consumerupdates/ucm612029.htm)

Tampons and cups are for menstrual bleeding only, not routine discharge (FDA, https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/products-and-medical-procedures/menstrual-product-options-facts-and-safe-use)

summary: Frequency can be a UTI symptom (NIDDK) or part of overactive bladder. For UTI-related frequency, treating the infection and short-term phenazopyridine help. For non-infectious frequency, MedlinePlus and NIDDK list bladder training with a bladder diary, pelvic floor (Kegel) exercises, limiting excess fluid/caffeine, then prescription bladder-relaxing medicines and electrical nerve stimulation if these fail.

summary: Urgency with burning suggests UTI (NIDDK) and is relieved by treating the infection, with phenazopyridine for short-term symptom relief. Non-infectious urgency (overactive bladder/urge incontinence) is managed first with bladder training, urge-suppression techniques (distraction, slow breathing, quick pelvic squeezes) and Kegels, then prescription medicines, Botox or electrical nerve stimulation when these do not help (NIDDK).

summary: The AUA/CUA/SUFU guideline (2025 amendment) says clinicians should offer cranberry for prophylaxis (moderate recommendation, grade B evidence), should tell patients D-mannose alone may not be effective (grade B), may offer methenamine hippurate (conditional) and increased water if intake is under 1.5 L/day, and should recommend vaginal estrogen for peri/postmenopausal women (grade B); antibiotic prophylaxis is also an option. Cochrane 2023 (50 trials) found cranberry probably reduces culture-verified UTIs in women with recurrent UTI (RR 0.74, moderate certainty) but not in pregnancy. Cochrane 2022 found very-low-certainty evidence for D-mannose, and a 2024 RCT (Hayward, JAMA Intern Med, 2 g/day) found no benefit. The guideline also asks for urinalysis and culture with each episode, with self-start treatment for selected patients.

urinalysis + culture each episode; self-start therapy for selected patients

caution: Cranberry did not reduce UTIs in pregnant women (Cochrane 2023, low certainty); ask a clinician before supplement doses in pregnancy or breastfeeding (NCCIH cranberry)

summary: NIDDK and MedlinePlus describe stepwise care: lifestyle change, bladder training, and pelvic floor muscle training (women who trained had fewer leaks per day; benefit appears after 4-6 weeks to several months and must be kept up). Biofeedback or electrical stimulation can help women learn correct Kegel technique; electrical nerve stimulation is used for urgency incontinence when other measures fail. Pessaries and tampon-like urethral inserts reduce stress leaks; absorbent pads, liners, washable or disposable underwear and skin barrier creams are established containment tools. Medicines, bulking agents and sling surgery come later.

summary: Non-hormonal vaginal moisturizers (used regularly) and lubricants (used during sex) are the first-line, mainstay options for vaginal dryness per The Menopause Society/ISSWSH, though OTC product evidence is limited and one 12-week RCT found moisturizer no better than placebo gel. Hyaluronic acid gels have been associated with reduced dryness. Low-dose vaginal estrogen or vaginal DHEA (prescription) is the most effective treatment for menopausal dryness. Prefer products with near-physiologic pH (3.8-4.5) and osmolality under 1,200 mOsm/kg (WHO).

effective_types.type: low-dose vaginal estrogen or vaginal DHEA (Rx)
regular sexual stimulation incl. with a device; pelvic floor PT; dilators

caution: Avoid products with glycerin, parabens, propylene glycol, warming agents, flavors, or spermicides; they may irritate vulvovaginal tissue (NAMS/ISSWSH 2018: https://menopause.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Management_of_genitourinary_syndrome_of_menopause.97565-2.pdf)
Oil-based products may damage latex condoms and may increase vaginal infection risk (Menopause Society MenoNote: https://menopause.org/wp-content/uploads/for-women/MenoNote-GSM.pdf)
Most commercial lubricants are hyperosmolar (2,000-6,000 mOsm/kg); WHO advises under 1,200 mOsm/kg and pH about 4.5 for vaginal use (https://extranet.who.int/prequal/node/31776)
Compounded vaginal hormones are not recommended (Menopause Society: https://menopause.org/wp-content/uploads/for-women/MenoNote-GSM.pdf)

Urinary burning or urgency or recurrent UTIs alongside dryness (Menopause Society: https://menopause.org/wp-content/uploads/for-women/MenoNote-GSM.pdf)

summary: Itching or irritation is commonly caused by yeast infection, trichomoniasis, menopause-related thinning, or contact irritation from sprays, douches, scented soaps, detergents and spermicides. Removing irritants and washing the vulva with plain warm water is the main self-care step; OTC azole antifungals are for yeast only. There is no good evidence that botanical vulvar balms treat irritation, and fragranced/botanical ingredients can themselves irritate.

OTC topical azole antifungal (if recurrent familiar yeast symptoms)

summary: Normal discharge is clear or white and changes through the cycle; gray thin fishy discharge suggests BV, thick white cottage-cheese discharge suggests yeast, and yellow/green or frothy discharge suggests trichomoniasis, gonorrhea or chlamydia. These need different treatments (antibiotics, antifungals) so a change in discharge warrants evaluation. A home pH test can help triage but cannot tell infections apart. Douching is not recommended.

caution: Douching can upset the vaginal flora and lead to infection (Cleveland Clinic: https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/symptoms/4719-vaginal-discharge)

summary: Some vaginal odor is normal; a new strong fishy odor (often worse after sex) is a hallmark of BV, and trichomoniasis or a retained tampon can also cause odor. BV requires prescription antibiotics (metronidazole, clindamycin). No data support douching, and NHS advises avoiding vaginal washes, deodorants and douches; there are no OTC treatments for elevated vaginal pH (FDA).

avoid douches, vaginal washes, deodorants and scented products; plain water washing
boric acid (only within recurrent BV regimens)

summary: CDC-recommended BV treatment is prescription metronidazole (oral or gel) or clindamycin cream; alternatives include secnidazole and tinidazole. For multiple recurrences, limited data support oral nitroimidazole followed by vaginal boric acid 600 mg daily for 21 days, then twice-weekly metronidazole gel for 4-6 months. CDC states no studies support probiotics/lactobacillus as adjunct or replacement therapy, and douching may increase relapse. Diagnosis uses Amsel criteria (including pH > 4.5) or Gram stain.

vaginal boric acid 600 mg x 21 days after antibiotics, for multiple recurrences

summary: Uncomplicated yeast infections are treated with OTC topical azoles (miconazole, clotrimazole, tioconazole) for 1-7 days or prescription oral fluconazole. Recurrent infections (3+ per year) use 6 months of weekly fluconazole. Boric acid 600 mg vaginally daily for 3 weeks is indicated only for recurrent non-albicans infections (about 70% eradication). In pregnancy only 7-day topical azoles are recommended. Mayo states no alternative therapies have been proved to treat yeast infections.
